name: Red Sweat Mystery
description: Eastern flight attendants report unexplained red/pink spotting; learner-safe PA practice.

pre.oneLine: Eastern Airlines flight attendants have red sweat.
pre.proof:
LEARNER CASE BRIEF — RED SWEAT MYSTERY
Eastern Airlines received reports of flight attendants noticing a temporary reddish or pink fluid or marking on exposed skin while on duty. The cause has not been established.

REPORTED COMPARISONS
• Flight attendants are the reported group. Lead flight attendants, pilots and passengers are not reported affected.
• Most reports involve Eastern A300 aircraft, with a few aboard other Eastern aircraft. No cases were reported on Eastern DC9 aircraft or other airlines.
• Reported body sites include face, hands and neck.
• In affected flights, the signs begin within roughly 30 minutes after takeoff and are short-lived.

BACKGROUND FOR INVESTIGATION
Eastern A300 operations introduced multiple unfamiliar materials or practices, including cleaning agents, surface coatings, cart/rack plastics, passenger safety-demonstration equipment and an experimental air-filter cartridge. Crews were trained on new life-vest demonstrations ahead of January A300 operations. A300 aircraft also replaced older equipment on many routes involving travel over water. Several medical and environmental explanations had already been considered without a conclusion.

YOUR TASK
Using only the reported facts, refine the Problem Statement and IS / IS NOT specification. Identify Distinctions and date relevant Changes. Propose mechanisms, destructively test candidate causes against the entire specification, and recommend a confirmation method. Do not assume that a new feature is automatically the cause.

Source: summarized and paraphrased from KT's PSDM participant case dossier; not the complete official case handout. Later solution/debrief intentionally excluded.

pre.healthy: Normal perspiration without unexplained reddish or pink spotting.
pre.now: Temporary red/pink fluid or marks on exposed skin during flight.

impact.now: HISTORICAL CASE: Eastern flight attendants reported temporary red/pink fluid or markings on exposed skin in flight. Crew discomfort, the true substance and any adverse medical effect were initially unresolved. The available case provides no verified injury count, flight interruption, passenger impact or severity classification (NMD).
impact.future: ILLUSTRATIVE OPERATIONAL CONCERN, not a reported outcome: if an unidentified substance remains on cabin-crew skin, continued exposure reports and unnecessary disruption are possible. Medical and cabin-safety implications require qualified review; do not assert injury, aircraft unserviceability or passenger exposure without evidence.
impact.time: On affected flights, symptoms began within approximately 30 minutes after takeoff and were short-lived. A300/new demonstration-vest preparation occurred before January 1980 operations; the newspaper-style report is from early March 1980. Exact first incident, decision deadline and closure timestamps: NMD.

ops.containDesc: HISTORICAL POST-EXERCISE RESULT: case resolution reports that the red-sweat reports stopped after Eastern removed the new demonstration life vests. This is not evidence of a formal major-incident declaration, bridge or medical outcome. NMD: who directed removal, exact date and independent monitoring duration.

table.note: Define the object and its factual deviation.

table.q: WHAT — Which specific people have the reported deviation?
table.is: Working Eastern Airlines flight attendants on affected flights.
table.no: Lead flight attendants, pilots and passengers are not reported affected.
table.di: Working attendants conduct cabin safety demonstrations and physically handle demonstration life vests; pilots and passengers do not. Whether unaffected lead attendants handled the same equipment is NMD and must be checked.
table.ch: New demonstration life vests introduced for A300 crews, with training before January 1980 flights (early January 1980; exact date NMD).

table.is: Temporary red/pink fluid or spotting resembling reddish sweat.

table.note: Locate the symptoms, the affected operation and close comparisons.

table.q: WHERE — On which aircraft, carrier or routes is the deviation reported?
table.is: Most reports are on Eastern A300 flights; a few involve other Eastern aircraft.
table.no: No reported cases on Eastern DC9 aircraft or other airlines; exact route-by-route comparison NMD.
table.di: Many Eastern A300s replaced older aircraft on routes involving travel over water, where water-evacuation life-vest demonstrations are used. This is a useful route/equipment difference to check against each affected and unaffected flight, not proof by itself.
table.ch: New life-vest demonstration equipment entered A300 service in early January 1980. New cleaning products, coatings and cart-rack plastics are additional candidate A300 Changes (dates NMD). Experimental air-filter cartridges were still being tested and entered full service later than the deviation; the date does not fit the onset.

table.q: WHERE — Where on the affected people is the deviation seen?
table.is: Exposed skin, including face, hands and neck.

table.note: Separate actual onset from publication date and possible changes.

table.q: WHEN — When was the deviation first observed?
table.is: The case was reported in early March 1980; the first occurrence date is NMD.

table.q: WHEN — What pattern has been observed since the first occurrence?
table.is: Several reported episodes; symptoms described as short-lived.

table.q: WHEN — When in the flight lifecycle does the deviation appear?
table.is: Reported onset is invariably within approximately the first 30 minutes after takeoff on affected flights.
table.no: No reported first-onset episodes beyond approximately 30 minutes after takeoff.
table.di: The predeparture safety demonstration is a concentrated equipment-handling opportunity before the early-flight symptom window; comparable later-flight activity does not involve that same initial demonstration. Match demonstration timing to each affected episode.
table.ch: The departure demonstration was a repeating activity; the relevant dated Change is the replacement/introduction of demonstration life vests in early January 1980, not a new change at the 30-minute mark.

table.note: Record only supported magnitude, size, count and trend facts.

table.is: Most reported cases involve A300 operations; total affected people and flights: NMD.

table.q: EXTENT — How much red/pink fluid or spotting is present in one occurrence?

table.is: NMD — occurrences per person not supplied.

causes.accusation: Shed flaking red ink while handled during the safety demonstration
causes.impact: Red pigment transfers to working attendants' exposed skin and perspiration spreads it into apparently red sweat shortly after takeoff
causes.summaryText: Newly introduced demonstration life vests shed red ink on handlers; perspiration smears the transferred pigment into the reported red/pink spots. This is the historical confirmed cause from the separate post-exercise reveal.
causes.evidence: POST-EXERCISE REVEAL / historical case outcome (not starting evidence): Flaking red ink from new demonstration vests transferred during over-water safety demonstrations; perspiration spread the pigment. Reports stopped after the demonstration vests were removed. For teaching, distinguish the Most Probable Cause from confirmed True Cause. Confirmation options: verify which crews/aircraft handled the new vests; observe transfer during a controlled demonstration; conduct a safe materials-transfer experiment; or replace/remove the defective demonstration equipment and monitor for nonrecurrence. Only the historical removal/outcome is reported, not any live testing by this workbook.

what-object.note: Working attendants' vest handling explains their exposure, unlike pilots/passengers. Check whether the unaffected lead attendants did not handle these same demonstration vests; that role-level comparison is not fully documented in the learner facts.

where-location.note: Over-water A300 safety demonstrations give a specific path for vest contact and the A300 concentration; verify vest distribution on the few affected other Eastern aircraft and the unaffected DC9/other-carrier flights. Aircraft type itself is not a cause.

when-description.note: Vest contact occurs at the departure demonstration, then perspiration can smear deposited ink soon after takeoff; this fits the first-30-minute onset rather than requiring a later in-flight exposure. The separate historical reveal confirms the red-ink transfer mechanism.

causes.accusation: Left red-tinted residue on crew-contacted surfaces
causes.impact: The residue transfers to working attendants' exposed skin and becomes visible as perspiration spreads it
causes.summaryText: A newly used A300 cleaner might deposit transferable red residue on surfaces handled by cabin crew, becoming visible with perspiration.
causes.evidence: UNCONFIRMED learner alternative. No evidence in the available participant dossier establishes that a cleaning product contains red pigment, affects only demonstrators, or was used on all affected aircraft. Compare actual products, dates, surfaces and affected/unaffected flights before treating this as causal.

what-object.note: Requires working attendants, but not pilots, passengers or lead attendants, to contact the residue-bearing surfaces. The role/exposure split has not been established.

where-location.note: A300-specific cleaner might explain many A300 reports, but needs evidence that the affected non-A300 Eastern flights also used it and the DC9/other-carrier comparison flights did not.

when-description.note: Requires contact shortly before takeoff and red residue that becomes visible rapidly with sweat; neither the contact timing nor red-staining chemistry has been demonstrated.

causes.suspect: New A300 service-cart or rack plastics
causes.accusation: Released transferable colored residue when cabin crew handled service equipment
causes.impact: Color transfers to exposed skin during preparation and becomes visible as the crew perspire
causes.summaryText: New cart/rack plastics might transfer colored material to attendants handling equipment and appear as red spotting after departure.
causes.evidence: UNCONFIRMED learner alternative. An A300 equipment difference could generate a hypothesis, but the material must actually shed red pigment, and the hypothesis must still fit other Eastern aircraft, unaffected lead attendants, and onset timing.

what-object.note: Assumes only affected working attendants handled the residue-bearing carts/racks and unaffected lead attendants did not; verify actual handling roles.

where-location.note: Needs evidence of the same plastic on a few affected non-A300 flights but absence on Eastern DC9 and unaffected carriers; no such fleet inventory is supplied.

when-description.note: Requires handling the cart/rack before or immediately after takeoff rather than later during cabin service, plus evidence of red pigment transfer.

causes.accusation: Failed to screen ozone, producing an airborne skin reaction
causes.impact: Cabin-air exposure would supposedly cause red/pink skin moisture during flight
causes.summaryText: An experimental air-filter change might alter cabin air and cause a skin reaction, but this explanation conflicts with crew specificity and with the dated filter rollout.
causes.evidence: REJECTED by destructive testing and timing. Instructor guidance says the cartridges were still being tested and were not fully implemented until after the deviation began. A later rollout cannot explain the earlier reports, regardless of whether ozone could produce this visible effect.

what-object.note: A shared cabin-air exposure would not naturally explain why affected working attendants develop red spots while nearby pilots, lead attendants and passengers do not. There is no supported role-specific ozone mechanism.

where-location.note: Assumes the trial cartridges are unique to affected A300s and also somehow account for the few affected non-A300 Eastern aircraft; verify installations rather than equating 'A300' with a causal filter.

when-description.note: Cabin air would remain present beyond the first 30 minutes, while the deviation is reported only at early onset. More decisively, the filter implementation occurred after the problem started, so the dated Change cannot be causal.

items.summary: Compare life-vest demonstration exposure by crew role and flight
items.detail: Proposed confirmation of the remaining WHAT/WHERE assumptions: compare which working attendants and lead attendants actually handled the new demonstration vests; then map affected A300 and other Eastern flights against routes, DC9 comparisons and the demonstration-vest inventory. Preserve both IS and close IS NOT facts.

decisionAnalysis.decision: ILLUSTRATIVE EXERCISE: how should an operator safely isolate the most probable pigment source while maintaining mandatory life-vest safety demonstrations?
decisionAnalysis.options:
A. Inspect new demonstration vests and substitute approved clean demo equipment one controlled change at a time; monitor matched flight reports.
B. Continue the same vests while investigating cabin air and cleaning agents (less diagnostic focus on crew handling).
C. Replace multiple new cabin products simultaneously (fast broad intervention but cause confirmation becomes ambiguous).
The historical case does not document a formal Decision Analysis or authorized alternative scoring.
decisionAnalysis.selectedOption: Illustrative recommendation: A — approved substitution and targeted investigation; historical reveal reports vest removal ended the complaints.
decisionAnalysis.ownerRole: Cabin Safety / Authorized Flight Operations (illustrative role)
decisionAnalysis.rationale: The role-specific contact pattern, over-water demonstrations, aircraft distribution and early-flight onset make vest pigment transfer the most defensible verification priority; this does not substitute for evidence from actual crew-activity and fleet inventories. An approved replacement preserves safety-critical demonstration capability and allows a more discriminating cause test than changing all cabin materials. Decision criteria include safety, reversibility, causal clarity and operational practicality. The case does not supply MUST/WANT scoring or real decision authority.

owner.name: Cabin Safety / Quality Lead (illustrative)
owner.notes: Proposed role for a modern training exercise. No named historical owner is documented.

risk.impactIfFails: ILLUSTRATIVE IF/THEN: IF suspect demonstration vests are removed without an approved substitute, THEN flight crews may lack required safety-demonstration equipment. IF several materials are changed at once, THEN a disappearance of symptoms does not uniquely confirm the true cause. Historical consequences of a poorly executed fix are NMD.
risk.prevent: Verify approved alternative demonstration equipment and operator authorization before removal; isolate one suspected variable at a time; preserve samples and a matched-flight case log; brief all affected crew roles. The 'Medium' risk rating is an exercise judgment, not a measured historical value.
risk.ifHappens: If the safety-demonstration replacement fails, stop the substitution and restore compliant equipment before flight. If red spotting recurs, return to the IS / IS NOT specification, check the affected lot and retest surviving causes rather than asserting resolution.

changeControl.rollbackPlan: ILLUSTRATIVE: authorized aviation-safety owner verifies replacement readiness; preserve traceable suspect specimens, approved replacement stock and a reversion plan. No specific historical rollback procedure is in the source.

verification.result: Approved safety demonstration remains effective, and follow-up flights with the suspect vests removed have no further red/pink spotting reports in matched crew/route/aircraft comparisons. Verify actual contact-transfer mechanism independently where practical; historical report states cessation after removal but lacks monitoring details.

current-state: HISTORICAL CASE RESOLUTION: the post-exercise reveal attributes red/pink spotting to flaking red ink from new demonstration life vests handled by flight attendants.
After those demonstration vests were removed, reports reportedly stopped; the case is not evidence of a live managed incident, formal closure or safety certification.
what-changed: New life-vest demonstration equipment and associated crew training preceded A300 operations in early January 1980.
Many affected Eastern A300 flights served over-water routes; other new materials were candidates but the filter full implementation came after onset.
Historical corrective change: removal of demonstration vests (exact date NMD).
remaining-risks: NMD: exact medical impact, fleet-wide exposure denominators, first symptom date, effect on lead attendants, and formal safety/approval records.

Illustrative response risk: never remove mandatory safety-demonstration capability without approved substitution; do not mistake nonrecurrence after multiple simultaneous changes for isolated confirmation.
must-watch-metrics: Count of new crew spotting reports per flight and crew role, aircraft type, route and safety-demonstration equipment lot.
Timing of spotting from takeoff and last equipment contact; document both affected and close unaffected crew.
Suspect-to-control pigment transfer and duration of symptom-free matched flights following a single controlled corrective change.
whats-next: Teaching debrief: connect each IS/IS NOT comparison to its factual Distinctions and dated Changes, then test all mechanisms destructively.
If adapting to a modern operation: authorize equipment checks, verify vest handling by role, conduct qualified non-human material inspection, ensure compliant substitutes, and monitor recurrence.
Do not treat these recommended actions as historical execution records; only vest removal and cessation are documented as the outcome.

notes.text: SOURCE / ROLE BOUNDARY. Participant starting evidence: PSDM participant workbook Red Sweat Mystery exercise (PDF pp. 80–83); official case-specific instructor notes: PSDM Instructor Reference Version H, printed pp. 331–338; separate participant post-exercise reveal (PDF pp. 130–131). This is a paraphrased course exemplar, not the full copyrighted handout or a real incident-management log.

MOST PROBABLE CAUSE vs TRUE CAUSE. Working flight attendants handle new demonstration life vests, red ink flakes onto exposed skin, and subsequent perspiration spreads it. Lead attendants' handling/nonhandling is a necessary comparison to verify; do not elevate that role assumption to a historical fact. The later official reveal identifies flaking red ink and cessation after vest removal as historical confirmation. The workbook's proposed experiments are examples, not documented field tests.

NMD = no meaningful data in the supplied case. Do not fabricate severity, named incident commander, bridge activation, response cadence, actual patient harm, quantitative case counts, exact occurrence/closure dates, measured air quality, or experimental results. False IS NOTs in earlier template drafts were cleared; a non-occurrence needs a close, factual comparator.

MAJOR INCIDENT FIELDS ARE AN ILLUSTRATIVE ADAPTATION: handover, decisions, PPA risk and corrective actions demonstrate what a full Intake source could contain if this happened today. They are not evidence that Eastern Airlines ran this ITIL-style incident process in 1980. Owner names are generic proposed roles, and blank date/time fields signify no verified timestamp.

CASE QUALITY: Spec IS / IS NOT first; find actual factual Distinctions (demonstration role/over-water route/early-flight lifecycle), date Changes (new vest demonstration equipment before January 1980 operations, filters too late), state testable complete mechanisms, identify assumptions rather than convert them to Y, and confirm through safe evidence/observation/experiment or single-change fix-and-monitor.
